## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta* (MN 137) is a discourse in the *Majjhimanikāya* providing a detailed analysis of the six sense fields (*saḷāyatana*) and their relationship to cognitive and emotional processes [SuttaCentral]. The text opens with an *uddesa* (summary statement) delineating the six internal sense bases, six external sense bases, six classes of consciousness, six classes of contact, eighteen kinds of mental exploration (*aṭṭhārasa manopavicārā*), thirty-six stances of beings (*chattiṃsa sattapadā*), the principle of relying on one mental quality to abandon another, the three applications of mindfulness (*tayo satipaṭṭhānā*) cultivated by a noble teacher, and the teacher as the supreme trainer of persons to be tamed (*yoggācariyānaṃ anuttaro purisadammasārathī*) [Stuart 2012].

Central to the sutta is the exploration of mental reactions across the six senses: perceptions producing joy (*somanassa*), grief (*domanassa*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*) [Stanley et al. 2018; Rogell 2003]. These eighteen explorations are differentiated into household-based attitudes (rooted in desire and attachment) and renunciation-based attitudes (rooted in spiritual insight), yielding thirty-six experiential positions [Hung 2010; Rogell 2003; Wen n.d.]. The sutta lays out a progressive path of overcoming: grief based on household life is abandoned by relying on grief based on renunciation, which is subsequently surmounted by joy based on renunciation, arising from seeing the impermanence of the senses [Hung 2010; Wen n.d.]. It also contrasts equanimity or neutral feeling bound to ignorance with equanimity grounded in wisdom [Anālayo 2006]. In addition, the discourse uniquely describes three *satipaṭṭhāna*s exercised by the Buddha as a teacher, who remains mindful and equanimous regardless of whether his disciples heed his teachings, ignore them, or respond unevenly [Stanley et al. 2018; Anālayo 2014; Anālayo 2017]. Later canonical and commentarial traditions treat this discourse as the sutta counterpart to the Abhidhamma analysis of *āyatana*s in the *Vibhaṅga* [Hazra 1994], and the *Papañcasūdanī* references it for the definitive categorization of worldly and unworldly feelings [Wen n.d.].

Curated parallels include a full discourse in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 163), *Taishō* 1536.9, *Arthaviniścayasūtra* 4, and Sanskrit Turfan fragments (SHT sutta 72) [SuttaCentral]. Its teaching on the three teacher's *satipaṭṭhāna*s is preserved in the Tibetan *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D4094), the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (D4092-2), and other northern scholastic treatises [Anālayo 2014; DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali Canon, close textual parallels and thematic relatives include AN 8.66, AN 8.120, AN 1.447–454, DN 15, DN 16, DN 33, DN 34, MN 77, and MN 148 (*Chachakka Sutta*) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus reveals substantial text reuse across 142 Pali texts, sharing extensive phrasing with AN 8 (matching AN 8.66), AN 10, AN 4, AN 6, and related *vibhaṅga* discourses of the *Majjhimanikāya* (MN 139 and MN 140) [DharmaNexus].
